title: Search for Diffuse Supernova Neutrino Background with 956.2 days of Super-Kamiokande Gadolinium Dataset

date.note: arXiv submission date; accepted by the Astrophysical Journal as of the fetched abstract page, no volume/page assigned yet.

significance.quote: No significant excess over background predictions was found in a DSNB spectrum-independent analysis, and 90\% C.L. upper limits on the astrophysical electron anti-neutrino flux were set.
significance.note: The abstract separately notes a spectral-fitting result with a ~1.2 sigma disagreement with the null-DSNB hypothesis, not a detection claim.

claim.quote: We report the search result for the Diffuse Supernova Neutrino Background (DSNB) in neutrino energies beyond 9.3 MeV in the gadolinium-loaded Super-Kamiokande (SK) detector with 22,500x956.2 m^3·day exposure.

summary.plain: Super-Kamiokande searched nearly three years of gadolinium-enhanced data for a faint, steady glow of neutrinos left over from every supernova that has ever exploded. No clear signal was found, but the search set the tightest limit yet on how bright that glow can be.
summary.technical: DSNB search using 552.2 days of SK-VI (0.01% Gd) and 404.0 days of SK-VII (0.03% Gd) data through September 2023, combining new machine-learning neutron-tagging with Gd, improved atmospheric-neutrino background rejection, and two parallel statistical analyses. No significant excess over background was found in the spectrum-independent analysis; 90% C.L. upper limits were set on the astrophysical electron-antineutrino flux above 9.3 MeV. A separate spectral fit showed a ~1.2σ preference over the null-DSNB hypothesis, consistent with an earlier 5823-day all-phase SK result.

why_it_matters: The diffuse supernova neutrino background is the relic glow of every core-collapse supernova in the observable universe; SK-Gd is the first detector generation built specifically to have a realistic chance of seeing it, and this is its most sensitive search to date.
